chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali al-Sa'iyy, who said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'May I be your ransom. I used to marry for Mut'ah (temporary marriage), but I disliked it and took it as an ill omen, so I gave Allah a pledge between the Rukn and the Maqam, and made a vow upon myself regarding that, including fasting, that I would not marry for Mut'ah. Then that became difficult for me, and I regretted my oath, and I did not have the financial means to marry publicly (permanent marriage). He said to me: 'You pledged to Allah that you would not obey Him? By Allah, if you do not obey Him, you will disobey Him.'

key_terms.الرُّكْنِ: The Rukn (a pillar of the Kaaba)
key_terms.الْمَقَامِ: The Maqam (Station of Abraham near the Kaaba)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on breaking a vow to stop temporary marriage (Mut'ah) if one lacks the means for permanent marriage?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, Ali al-Sa'iyy recounts his vow to abandon Mut'ah, to which Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) responded that since Mut'ah is a lawful act of obedience to Allah, abstaining from it constitutes disobedience. This highlights the Shia juristic principle that a vow to refrain from a permissible act (Mubah) is effectively a vow to disobey God, as the divine command is to utilize His provisions. The Imam’s concise reply underscores the theological link between legal permissibility and divine obedience in the context of personal vows.
